Family Health

Semen and sperm: the difference, production and test results

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Semen and sperm are closely connected, but they are not the same. Understanding the distinction makes questions about ejaculation, pregnancy prevention and semen testing easier to discuss without relying on appearance or fixed numerical rules.

Semen is fluid; sperm are cells

Semen is the mixture of fluid released during ejaculation. Sperm are microscopic reproductive cells that may be carried in it. These words describe different things, even though they are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation.

Most of the visible ejaculate comes from glands, not from the sperm cells themselves. Semen can contain very few sperm or none; a white appearance or an apparently usual amount cannot show whether someone is fertile. An orgasm with little or no visible fluid also does not reveal its cause without assessment.

What seminal fluid contains and does

The seminal vesicles and prostate provide much of the fluid, with contributions from other glands. The mixture includes water and substances such as sugars and proteins. For example, fructose from the seminal vesicles can provide energy for sperm. The presence of nutrients does not make semen a nutritional treatment.

Fluid helps carry sperm out through the urethra, and each sperm has a tail that enables its own movement. Movement through the female reproductive tract also depends on its environment and transport mechanisms, not simply on the amount of semen.

Where sperm and semen come from

Sperm develop in the seminiferous tubules inside the testes and undergo further maturation in the epididymis, a coiled structure beside each testis. During ejaculation, they travel through the vas deferens and mix with glandular secretions before leaving through the urethra. Testes also produce testosterone through different cells.

The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder. The prostate lies below the bladder and surrounds part of the urethra. The bulbourethral glands contribute lubricating secretions during arousal. This shared route does not mean urine and semen are the same fluid.

Sperm are too small to identify by eye

A sperm cell has a head carrying genetic material, a midpiece and a long tail. The head is much smaller than the whole cell, which includes that tail. Microscopy is needed to see and assess these cells.

Looking at semen, including its thickness, color or apparent amount, cannot count sperm or assess their movement and shape. A laboratory semen analysis measures several features together. Home observation is not a substitute for that assessment.

Why the amount of semen varies

Ejaculate volume varies between people and between samples. The interval since ejaculation, collection completeness, age, health and some medicines can affect the result. A teaspoon is not a required amount, and there is no universal early-thirties peak that determines an individual’s fertility.

Volume and sperm concentration are different measurements. More fluid does not automatically mean more sperm or a better chance of pregnancy. Follow the laboratory’s collection instructions, including its requested interval without ejaculation; tell the laboratory if part of the sample was missed. Do not stop prescribed medicines to change a result.

Concentration, total count and reference values

Concentration means sperm per milliliter; total count means the number in the whole ejaculate. The EAU table based on WHO’s 2021 reference data lists lower fifth-centile values of 16 million sperm/mL, 39 million per ejaculate and 1.4 mL volume. These describe a reference population, not an average or a pass/fail fertility test.

Someone below a reference value may conceive, and someone above it may still have difficulty. No single count proves fertility or infertility. Clinicians consider movement, shape, history and the other partner’s reproductive health. A finding of no sperm is called azoospermia and needs proper investigation; an unexpected result may require a repeat sample, with timing chosen by the clinic.

Pre-ejaculate can carry sperm

Pre-ejaculatory fluid appears during arousal before ejaculation. Although the secreting glands do not manufacture sperm, samples can contain them, including moving sperm. A small 2011 volunteer study demonstrated this but cannot tell an individual their chance of pregnancy. It is unsafe to assume that sperm can only be left over from a previous ejaculation.

Urinating after an earlier ejaculation does not guarantee sperm-free pre-ejaculate. Withdrawal is not a reliable way to rule out pregnancy. Put a condom on before genital contact and use it correctly throughout sex if that is your chosen protection; condoms also reduce STI transmission. After possible unprotected exposure, seek emergency-contraception advice promptly rather than trying saliva or water.

How long sperm may survive

In favorable conditions in the female reproductive tract, sperm can remain capable of fertilization for up to about five days. This helps explain why the fertile window includes days before ovulation. It does not mean all sperm survive five days in the vagina or that an app can identify a guaranteed safe day.

Outside the body, conditions such as drying and temperature matter, so there is no dependable universal countdown in minutes. Wet semen reaching the vulva or vagina, including on fingers or toys, can pose a pregnancy risk. Washing, saliva, a bath or having sex in water is not contraception after genital exposure; seek timely advice if worried.

Production and maturation take time

Making and maturing sperm takes more than 70 days, often described as roughly two to three months. This is an approximate biological process, not a promise that every person produces an entirely new, healthy supply exactly 74 days after a change. Illness and medicines can affect later samples.

Sperm production is ongoing in many people after puberty, but ejaculation does not switch it off or permanently use up a fixed lifetime supply. When trying to conceive, regular intercourse is generally more useful than prolonged abstinence to save sperm. Use the clinic’s specific collection instructions when preparing a test.

Age and health can affect production

Many people continue to produce sperm into later life, but production is not guaranteed to continue unchanged until death. Hormonal problems, testicular disease or injury, some cancer treatments, genetic conditions and other factors can reduce or stop it. Age-related changes vary; there is no universal switch at age 50.

Smoking, recreational drugs and some medicines may affect reproductive health. External testosterone and anabolic steroids can suppress sperm production and are not a fertility treatment. Discuss the exact products and your reproductive plans with a clinician; do not abruptly stop prescribed treatment or assume supplements can repair a low count.

When to request assessment

For pregnancy planning, seek assessment after a year of regular unprotected sex, or earlier when there is a known risk or concern. ASRM advises earlier evaluation after six months when the partner providing eggs is 35 or older. Both partners may need assessment. Repeated little or no ejaculate, painful ejaculation or possible infection also warrant clinical advice. A new testicular lump or swelling needs urgent clinician assessment. Blood in semen should be checked at an appointment.

Sudden severe testicular pain, testicular pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a routine semen test or assume it is harmless because the amount of semen looks usual. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the clinic what each semen-test measurement means and whether a repeat sample or assessment of both partners is needed. Follow collection instructions and disclose medicines and missed sample portions.

Use appropriate contraception from the start of genital contact if avoiding pregnancy. Seek prompt emergency-contraception advice after possible exposure; do not rely on withdrawal, urination, saliva or water.

Discuss persistent ejaculation changes, pain, lumps, possible infection or fertility concerns. Seek emergency help immediately for the testicular-pain warning signs above.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record symptoms, medicines, test dates and questions for an appointment. It cannot count sperm, interpret fertility from a photograph, diagnose a cause or provide contraception. Symptoms and professional advice take priority over an app estimate.

When to seek help

Do not self-start testosterone, fertility supplements or antibiotics, or stop prescribed medicines to alter semen. Seek immediate emergency assessment for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or at rest. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance. Possible unprotected exposure needs timely contraception advice; a normal-looking ejaculate does not rule out pregnancy risk or fertility problems.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Semen is mainly glandular fluid; sperm are microscopic cells that may be carried in it.
  • A usual-looking amount cannot show sperm count, movement or fertility. Reference values are not a pass/fail test.
  • Pre-ejaculate can contain sperm. Urinating, withdrawal, saliva and water do not guarantee pregnancy prevention.
  • Sperm development takes roughly months; health, treatment and age can affect production. Discuss concerns rather than self-treating.

Frequently asked questions

Does pre-ejaculate contain sperm?

It can, including moving sperm. The amount varies and cannot be judged by looking. Urinating after an earlier ejaculation does not guarantee it is sperm-free; use appropriate contraception from the start of genital contact.

How many sperm are released during ejaculation?

The total depends on concentration and volume. A laboratory measures both, along with movement and shape. The WHO2021-based lower reference values are 16 million/mL and 39 million per ejaculate; neither is a personal fertility guarantee or a diagnostic cutoff by itself.

How long does making sperm take?

Development and maturation take more than 70 days, roughly two to three months. It is an approximate process rather than an exact 74-day reset, and illness or medicines can affect later samples.

Does the body ever stop producing sperm?

It may. Many people continue later in life, but disease, hormonal changes, treatments and other factors can reduce or stop production. There is no guarantee of unchanged lifelong production or one age at which it always stops.

Can semen contain no sperm?

Yes. Semen is largely glandular fluid, so sperm may be absent despite a visible ejaculate. Confirmed azoospermia requires clinical investigation; appearance cannot diagnose it.

Can sperm survive five days outside the body?

The often-quoted five days refers to favorable conditions within the female reproductive tract, not a dry surface or a universal time in the vagina. Outside-body conditions vary. Wet semen reaching the vulva or vagina can still pose a pregnancy risk; ask promptly about emergency contraception after possible exposure.

Does a larger amount mean better fertility?

No. Volume is different from concentration, total count, movement and shape. A clinician interprets these together with both partners’ history. Follow collection instructions and report a missed portion rather than judging fertility by a teaspoon estimate.

When is testicular pain an emergency?

Seek immediate emergency assessment for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting more than an hour or continuing at rest. Do not wait for a routine scan or semen analysis. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
